prize_parts.citation: for the discovery of the neutrino mixing angle theta-13 through the disappearance of reactor antineutrinos

statement.case_for: The reactor measurement of theta-13 is the kind of result I put first: a clue from nature that nobody could have deduced by thought alone. The last unknown angle of the neutrino mixing matrix turned out to be large, around nine degrees, and that single number is what makes leptonic CP violation and the mass ordering experimentally reachable at all. It is the reason DUNE, Hyper-Kamiokande and JUNO are built the way they are. The discovery was nearly simultaneous in Daya Bay and RENO, quickly cross-checked by Double Chooz and by the T2K and MINOS appearance data, and has been refined for over a decade within a stable three-flavour framework. There is no maturity question and no interpretational dispute, and the 'existential' dimension, why matter beats antimatter, is not far away.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is overlap and credit. The 2015 prize already honoured neutrino oscillations, so some colleagues will see theta-13 as a follow-on measurement of a known phenomenon rather than a new discovery. Credit is also spread across several collaborations: Double Chooz leadership, and the accelerator appearance results, are outside the three credited names, and recognising spokespersons of collaborations of hundreds is always a statement about leadership more than authorship. Finally, the opening shows that only Mark Pearce and I ranked it in the top eight, so it has the thinnest breadth of support of any of my top candidates, and I should not mistake my own enthusiasm for committee-level merit.

responses.point: Pearce ranked IceCube first and theta-13 second, stressing that the astrophysical neutrino flux opens a new window, while noting that a one-person award for a very large collaboration is contestable and that the Double Chooz exclusion is a judgement call.
responses.response: I agree with the second half completely and it is why I would not put Halzen alone at the top: a single name for a collaboration of hundreds, with AMANDA-era colleagues and the TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 analyses authored by many, will be hard to defend, and independent confirmation by a second large telescope is still thin. I also take his point about Double Chooz. Where I differ is that the theta-13 result is already fully mature and its priority story, Daya Bay and RENO announcing within weeks of each other, is simpler than the IceCube internal history. If the committee wants a neutrino prize, I would accept IceCube only once the source identification is firmer; for now it is my first alternative on discovery grounds only after B048.

responses.point: Kroll ranked optical lattice clocks first: original idea, unambiguous performance near 1e-18, independent confirmation in many national laboratories, and a path to redefining the second, with a clean two-person credit.
responses.response: I ranked B049 eighth and I should explain why, since the credit is cleaner than for any other candidate and I do not dispute the engineering. My reservation is that a clock is a superb instrument, but the discovery content, something new about nature, is so far a null result on constants and a promise on geodesy. The 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes also covered much of the underlying conceptual ground. I accept, however, that six of eight members ranked it, and if the clock yields a measured time dilation or constants drift that surprises us I would revise sharply. I will keep it on the table but not put it above a measurement that has already changed what the whole neutrino programme looks for.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect first as a case where band topology and protected edge states produce measurable behaviour, with Kane and Mele for theory and Molenkamp for the decisive HgTe experiment.
responses.response: I ranked B048 second and share the scientific assessment: it is a genuinely new concept confirmed in HgTe and in many compounds, with fifteen years of replication. Where I want to push back, gently, is on the credit. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicted the HgTe realisation that Molenkamp then observed, and Zhang is deceased, so the experimental pairing is less symmetric than the credited trio suggests, and the 3D topological insulator work of Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents and Hasan blurs the boundary. Eriksson's theory-plus-decisive-experiment argument is a fair solution, but I would like the committee to be explicit that the prize rewards the quantum spin Hall effect and not all of topological matter. This is why I consider it my best alternative to theta-13 rather than a rival.

responses.point: Johansson ranked circuit QED first, arguing that strong coupling of a superconducting artificial atom to a single microwave photon is a basic, robust discovery, while acknowledging proximity to the community and overlap with the 2025 prize.
responses.response: I appreciate the candour about possible bias; that is the right way to raise it. Scientifically I find the strong-coupling result convincing and mature. My concern is timing and allocation: the 2025 prize was for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits, and rewarding the same platform one year later, with four contested names for three places (Blais, Wallraff, Schoelkopf, Girvin), would invite the criticism that we are rewarding a technology cluster. Only Johansson ranked it at all, so I would want to hear from the others whether they see cQED as distinct enough before I could support it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee considers theta-13 a sufficiently distinct discovery from the 2015 neutrino-oscillation prize.
Whether excluding Double Chooz and accelerator-appearance leaders is acceptable, or whether the credit story is incomplete; I rely on memory for individual roles.
Breadth of support: only two members ranked B024 in the top eight, so the discussion may legitimately move toward B049 or B048.
Whether the quantum spin Hall prize can be defined cleanly without Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile for the shortlisted candidates. My PhD supervisor David Gross, my collaborator Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala string group are not connected to any of them. I am a theorist from outside every shortlisted field, and I treat that as a reason to defer to specialists on technical points rather than a conflict.
